activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: In the Scripps National Spelling Bee, a speller may start over, but changing any letters already said counts as a misspelling.
story:
Charlotte stood at the kitchen counter holding a stack of index cards, her lips moving around the word "chrysanthemum" for the tenth time that afternoon. Ira sat on the stool across from her with the list of practice words, and Cash had appointed himself judge, holding a wooden spoon like a microphone. The county spelling bee was in nine days, and the winner would advance to the regionals, then possibly to the Scripps National Spelling Bee itself, which was the whole reason the rules sheet from Mr. Friedman was taped to the refrigerator.

Last year, in the school gym, Charlotte had learned something the hard way. She could still see it: the microphone, the paper cup of water, the word "separate." She had begun, "S-E-P..." and then, halfway through, realized the second vowel was wrong. Without pausing, she had slipped an "a" in place of the "e" she'd already said, hoping nobody noticed. The judges noticed. The bell had rung, and she had walked back to her folding chair with her ears burning.

"C-A-F..." Cash began reading.

"Wait," Charlotte said. "Before we start, can we do it exactly like a real bee? Full rules." She pulled the sheet off the fridge and read it carefully, her finger moving down the page. Then she stopped. "Huh. It says you can start over."

Ira leaned over to look. "Start over how?"

"You can say the word, then begin spelling again from the beginning. But listen to this part." She read it out loud. "Changing any letters already said counts as a misspelling." She set the paper down slowly. "So that's what happened to me last year. I didn't get knocked out because I said the wrong letter. I got knocked out because I changed one I'd already said."

"That seems harsh," Ira said.

"Maybe. But at least now I know." Charlotte had spent a year thinking the bell was random, an illusion of bad luck, and the truth was stranger: the rule had been printed on a page she had never bothered to read. She picked up the wooden spoon from Cash and handed it back. "Okay. Call it."

For the next hour they drilled. When Charlotte stumbled on "ratatouille," she said the word again and restarted cleanly, keeping every letter she'd already spoken exactly the same. When Ira misspelled "rhubarb," he tried to justify it by claiming Cash had mumbled, and they all laughed, and Cash mumbled it again on purpose, worse. Ira restarted and got it right on the second try.

"Question," Ira said, flipping the card over. "What do you do if you're halfway through and you know it's wrong?"

Charlotte didn't answer right away. Then she squared her shoulders the way she imagined the resilient spellers on television did, the ones who got up after the bell and came back the next year. "I finish the word anyway, or I start over with the same letters. Either way, I say it out loud. No quiet fixes."

Cash raised the wooden spoon. "C-H-R-Y-S-A-N-T-H-E-M-U-M."

"Ring that bell," Charlotte said.

activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
knowledge_domain: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
fact: When unpaid interest is added to a debt, the next month's interest is charged on that interest too, so the debt grows faster over time.
story:
Emmett stood at the counter at Maple Street Bank, holding his cousin's credit card statement so tightly the paper crumpled at the corner. He had twenty-three dollars of birthday money in his pocket, and the skateboard he wanted cost one hundred and eighty. The plan had been simple: put the skateboard on the cousin's card, pay her back ten dollars a month. But the statement confused him. His cousin had stopped using the card three months ago, and the balance had still gone up each month. It was like watching a plant grow in a dark closet.

Amar leaned over his shoulder at the little table by the window, where a sign listed things the bank excluded from the safe deposit boxes, including flammable materials. "You're doing the face," Amar said. "The math face."

"It doesn't add up," Emmett said. He flattened the paper. "She owed two hundred and forty dollars. She paid twenty dollars last month. The balance now is two hundred twenty-three. That's more than two forty minus twenty."

Tatum slid into the third chair, shaking juice from her umbrella. "Let me see." She ran her finger down the columns. "There. Interest charged, eighteen dollars. But she paid twenty. That's only two dollars ahead."

"But last month's interest was seventeen something," Emmett said slowly. He turned the page over, then back, as if the answer might be hiding on the other side. "It's charging more each time. Why would it charge more if the debt is getting smaller?"

Ms. Çelik, who ran the branch and had once helped Emmett's mother set up a savings account, stopped at their table on her way past. Emmett held up the statement. "Why is her interest bigger now than before?"

She tapped the number with one red-nailed finger. "You've spotted it yourself, haven't you? Unpaid interest gets added to what she owes. Next month, the interest is charged on that interest too." Then she moved on to the drive-through window, because the little red light above it had begun to blink, the signal that a customer was waiting.

Emmett sat very still. The debt wasn't just sitting there. It was feeding itself. He took out his phone and opened the calculator, punching in ten dollars a month, month after month, watching the balance shrink slower and slower. At twenty dollars a month, the two hundred twenty-three would take more than a year to clear, and he would pay for the skateboard plus a whole extra month of charges.

"There's another way," Tatum said. "My brother saved first. Boring, but zero interest."

Emmett folded the statement and put it in his back pocket. Fifteen dollars a week from mowing the neighbor's lawn, and the skateboard would be his in twelve weeks, owing nobody anything. He slid his birthday money across the counter to the teller. "New savings account, please. Twenty-three dollars."

"Twenty-three dollars it is," the teller said, and slid the little blue passbook back to him.

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: When two identical bulbs are wired in series to one battery, each glows more dimly than a single bulb would on the same battery.
story:
Sebastian's model lighthouse was due on Friday, and by Tuesday it still had no light. He had cleared a corner of the garage, taped a diagram to the workbench, and laid out his supplies: a battery, a bulb, a switch he'd salvaged from a broken flashlight, and three wires with the ends twisted clean. His dad had an allergy to soldering fumes, so Sebastian had been banished to the garage with the door open and instructions to monitor the little space heater and switch it off if it started to smell funny.

Youcef came over after school and stood over the bench like a foreman. "So the light goes at the top of the tower."

"At the top. It's a lighthouse. That's the whole job of a lighthouse."

Sebastian clipped one wire from the battery to the switch, another from the switch to the bulb, and a third back to the battery. He flipped the switch and the bulb glowed, steady and yellow. Youcef applauded with one hand against the workbench.

"Too dim," Sebastian said, frowning at it. "You can barely see it across the garage. Ms. Andersen said the best project guides a ship. Mine could guide a moth, maybe."

"Put in another bulb," said Youcef. "Two bulbs, twice the light."

Sebastian had to admit that sounded reasonable, in the way that a lot of Youcef's ideas sounded reasonable. He twisted a second identical bulb in after the first, so both sat in a row between the switch and the battery, and flipped the switch again.

Both bulbs lit. Both bulbs were dimmer. Not just a little dimmer, either. Each one glowed weaker than the single bulb had on the same battery, like they were splitting something between them and neither got enough.

"That's backwards," Youcef said. "I want a refund."

"There's nothing to refund. It's the same battery." Sebastian lifted the wire between the two bulbs, then set it down. He unscrewed the second bulb, clipped the wire straight to the first one, and flipped the switch. The lone bulb glowed bright and sure, brighter than either of the two had managed. "When the two are wired in series, they both go dim. One bulb, full light."

"So less is more."

"I'm not putting that on the poster. Ms. Andersen will think we're being philosophical." He climbed the ladder and fixed the single bulb into the top of the tower, then crossed the garage to the far door, where the afternoon light was fading, and flipped the switch. The little beacon flared at the top of the lighthouse.

Youcef stood beside him in the dim garage. "Okay. Now find me a ship."

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: In the decimal coordinates used by GPS and online maps, latitudes south of the equator and longitudes west of the prime meridian are written as negative numbers.
story:
Rose slid the giant atlas off the shelf and dropped it onto the table with a thud that made Brielle look up from her book. Ms. Mehta had assigned them a scavenger hunt for Monday: give the location of a city using only numbers, no names allowed. Rose wanted Lima, because her grandmother had grown up there, and she was determined to get it exactly right.

She found Lima on the map of Peru and traced the faint curved lines with her finger until one crossed the city. "Latitude," she muttered, writing down 12.05. Then she followed a vertical line down to the numbers along the bottom. "And longitude, 77.04." At the next table, a poster announced a free flu vaccine clinic on Saturday, and a sign by the old map drawers read that the room's flammable film reels had been moved downstairs, but Rose barely noticed. She pulled out the library's laptop, opened the map site, and typed 12.05, 77.04 into the search box.

The map spun and landed on empty ocean. Rose stared. "That's not Lima. That's not even the right ocean." Brielle leaned over, chewing her pencil. "Try it again? Maybe you typed wrong." Rose retyped each digit slowly and got the same blue nothing. She sat back, tapping the pencil against her chin. Same numbers, different place. That could only imply that something about the numbers themselves was telling the map where to go, and not just the digits. She glanced at the atlas again, at the wide line labeled equator running across Peru's northern neighbor Colombia, with Lima below it, south of it. On the laptop screen, the ocean map showed coordinates in the corner: 12.05 N, 77.04 E. East? Lima wasn't east. It was west of the prime meridian line that ran through the atlas margin.

"Negative," Rose said suddenly. "South of the equator and west of that line, the numbers have to be negative." She typed 12.05, then a minus sign, then 77.04 with its own minus. The map whirled, and the streets of Lima bloomed across the screen, a red pin sitting right on the Plaza Mayor. Brielle laughed and copied the numbers onto her worksheet. "Okay, but explain the minus signs to me on the walk home." Rose closed the laptop and hugged the atlas to her chest. "Deal," she said. "But first, let's find your city."

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: By convention, a location's latitude is written first and its longitude second, as in about 40 degrees north, 74 degrees west for New York City.
story:
Charlie spread the city map across the kitchen table, weighed down the curling corners with salt shakers, and frowned at the note Paolo had sent her: "Check this. Amalia and I typed 74 north, 40 west into the map app for our New York project and it showed us a hunk of ice and rock nowhere near New York. Did the app break?"

Charlie tried it herself on her mom's tablet. Sure enough, the pin landed far, far away, in a barren stretch of nothing. She tried the opposite order, 40 north and 74 west, and the pin dropped right onto New York City. So the app worked fine. Something else was going on.

She remembered a flash of last week's geography class, when Ms. Munro had handed out sheets of translucent graph paper to lay over the atlas so the grid lines showed through the countries. "Latitude lines run sideways like a belt," Ms. Munro had said, "and longitude lines run up and down," and then she'd said something about the order you write them in, but Charlie had been busy drawing a mustache on the explorer in her textbook and had missed it. Now she squinted at her notes. Somewhere there was a rule, and she had a hunch. She grabbed a pencil and wrote "about 40 degrees north, 74 degrees west" beside "New York City," then wrote it flipped beside the icy pin. The flipped version matched Paolo's mistake exactly.

"Paolo!" she said when he and Amalia arrived with the poster board and Amalia's emergency snack of cheese crackers. "The app didn't break. You swapped them."

"Swapped what?" Paolo said, mouth full.

"The numbers. Latitude goes first, then longitude. That's why your pin ended up in the frozen middle of nowhere." She slid the tablet over so they could see both pins side by side.

Amalia leaned in, tapping the New York pin twice. "So the rule is latitude first, always?"

"Latitude first, longitude second," Charlie said. "Try it."

Amalia typed the coordinates in the proper order, and the pin obediently landed on Manhattan. Paolo threw his arms up like he'd scored a goal, nearly knocking over a salt shaker.

"For the poster," Charlie said, pulling out Ms. Munro's translucent grid sheet and laying it over the map so they could trace the lines, "we can show the rule with a prototype, just one little worked example, and let people generate their own guesses for other cities. Ms. Munro will love it."

"Or we draw a tiny mustache on this explorer too," Paolo said, pointing at the textbook still sitting open on the counter.

"Paolo. Poster first." Amalia uncapped the glue.

Charlie smiled, lined up the ruler, and drew the first grid line straight across the map.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Fresh sweat has almost no smell; body odor comes from bacteria on the skin breaking down sweat.
story:
The locker room bathroom smelled like wet towels and floor cleaner, and Louis stood at the sink with his shirt pulled up over his nose. Timothe was already complaining, holding his jersey at arm's length like it might be flammable, which it probably was, being polyester.

"Your sweat reeks," Timothe said.

"It can't be the sweat itself," Louis said. "Fresh sweat has almost no smell."

Jenny leaned against the doorframe, still holding her water bottle. "Then what stinks?"

Louis had read the back of his deodorant stick that morning, the whole little paragraph on the label, and he was starting to think it might actually be true. "Body odor comes from bacteria on your skin breaking down the sweat. Tiny living things. They eat it, and the smell is, like, what's left over."

"That's disgusting," Timothe said.

"That's amazing," Jenny said.

Louis decided to test it, because a claim like that shouldn't just be believed. He ran hot water, washed one armpit thoroughly with soap, dried it, and left the other one alone. Then he waited. While he waited he told them about his plan to boycott morning showers for the whole summer, which had lasted exactly two days before his mother had staged an intervention involving the garden hose.

"Now smell," he said, pointing at the unwashed side, then the washed one. Timothe leaned in like a scientist, grimaced at the first, and blinked at the second.

"Nothing," Timothe said. "The clean one smells like nothing."

"That's the technique," Louis said. "Soap gets rid of the bacteria, not the sweat. You could sweat all day and it wouldn't matter, as long as they're not there to break it down."

Timothe had been insisting for ten minutes that some people just had stinky sweat and nothing could be done, and now he stood there with his mouth slightly open, revising. He picked up his jersey, sniffed it, and dropped it in the sink and turned on the tap.

"Coach is going to think I've gone soft," he said, scrubbing.

"Coach," said Jenny, "is going to thank us."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: A control group in an experiment gets everything the test group gets except the thing being tested, so any difference between the groups can be linked to that one thing.
story:
The note from his mother said, "Buy the plant tonic for the window boxes, and don't forget Kaylie's birthday card." Noah folded the note into his pocket and counted his allowance on the walk to Shapiro's Pharmacy, which sold everything from cough drops to flower food.

He found the tonic on a bottom shelf, its label showing a robust tomato plant twice the size of a sad one beside it. Kaylie was already there, examining the same bottle. "You should get it," she said. "My cousin Ruby used it on her balcony garden last summer, and by August her beans were up to the railing." Noah remembered his own beans from the spring, the ones he had watered with tonic every single week. They had climbed beautifully, and he had felt proud, until his grandmother's untended vines along the fence had climbed just as high without a drop of anything. That quiet resentment had stayed with him, a suspicion that his bottle had done nothing at all.

"But Ruby also watered, and it was sunny, and it was summer," Noah said slowly. "How do you know it was the tonic?" He stared at the label. What you needed, he realized, was two groups of plants that got everything the same except the one thing being tested. One row of beans watered with tonic, one row watered without it, side by side. Then any difference between them would point at the tonic and nothing else. "Like a control group," he said. "Everything the same except the one thing you're testing."

Mr. Shapiro came around the counter with a price sticker in his hand. "Control group, huh? Good thinking." He turned the bottle toward the light. "Might interest you to know, this tonic got recalled last month. It's water, food coloring, and a nice label. The company settled on Tuesday."

Kaylie laughed so hard she had to lean on the shelf. "Ruby is going to be furious." Noah put the bottle back and took out his mother's note. "Come on," he said. "If we plant two rows of beans, I'll race you to the railing."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: The U.S. Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 requires parental consent before websites collect personal information from children under 13, which is why many sites require users to be 13.
story:
Robyn's kitchen smelled like burnt toast, which Robyn claimed was on purpose. Gabriella sat at the counter with Robyn's phone while Robyn scraped the worst piece into the sink. On the screen was the signup page for Chirp, the app everyone at school had joined except the two of them, because Robyn's mother kept her password in a jar labeled "emergency cookies."

"Put my birthday in," Robyn said, "I want to see the part where you pick your bird."

Gabriella typed the date, and the screen turned red. You must be 13 or older to create an account. She tried again in case the phone had misread her, and it turned red again, the same flat little message. "It doesn't even say sorry," Gabriella said.

Robyn leaned over her shoulder. "So put a different year. Nobody checks."

"Then why do they ask?" Gabriella tapped the help link, mostly to seem busy while she thought. She scrolled past a lot of small print until she found a paragraph that mentioned an actual law, the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998, which said websites had to get parental consent before collecting personal information from children under 13. That was why so many sites drew the line at 13, the page said, plain as a stop sign.

"See, it's not a rule they made up to be annoying," Gabriella said. "It's the law. Under 13, they'd have to get your mom's permission first, like a permission slip."

"That's it? That's the whole reason everyone lies about their birthday on the internet?"

"Not lies. Adjustments." Gabriella entered 1998, and the screen turned green and asked her to choose a bird. She chose a lethargic-looking owl, mostly because it matched how she felt about the toast situation.

They spent a while testing the app, and Gabriella noticed something. Robyn typed messages in ALL CAPITALS, the way she talked, loud even in writing. When Gabriella wrote "that's hilarious" in lowercase, Robyn read it back in a wounded voice and asked why she was being so dry about it. Gabriella tried a single exclamation point, and Robyn perked up instantly. Same words, different weather. "You have to shout at me a little," Robyn said. "Or I can't hear you."

"Fine. THIS OWL IS HILARIOUS."

Later, when they tried to post a photo of the toast, a notice popped up asking who could see it, everyone, friends, or private. Robyn wanted everyone. "It's just toast," Gabriella said, "but the whole internet doesn't need toast." She set it to friends only, and the owl blinked on the screen as if agreeing. Robyn was already drafting her autobiography, which she kept calling her memoir, and the first line was "I survived breakfast." Gabriella couldn't refute that.

From the doorway, Robyn's mother said, "Whose phone is that?"

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: Counting up is a quick way to check change: start at the price and add each coin and note handed back until you reach the amount you paid.
story:
Nolan sat on the bus stop bench outside the corner store and read his mother's note a third time. "Milk, two percent, one litre. Money in the front pocket. You can do this." The last part had been underlined twice, which was either encouraging or a warning. Spencer stood beside him, hands in his hoodie, watching the traffic like it was a frontier he had no plans to cross. "I'll wait here," Spencer said. "Somebody has to hold the bench down."

The first time Nolan had tried this, two weeks ago, he had made it to the door and then turned around and walked home with the money still in his pocket, telling his mother the store had been out of milk. That story had been, at best, plausible, and she had not believed it for a second. Since then he had been practising. He knew the route, he knew the milk was on the second shelf, and he knew that if he did this today, he would finally conquer the corner store, at least in his own mind.

Inside, he found the milk without trouble and carried it to the counter, where a small kid was already standing in front of the cashier, frowning at a pile of coins in his palm. The kid had paid with a five for a chocolate bar that cost two dollars sixty. The cashier had handed back two dollars forty, and the kid clearly did not trust it. He counted his coins one at a time, lost his place, and started over.

Nolan watched the kid try again, and something clicked into place. "Try counting up," Nolan said. "Start at the price, then add each coin you got back until you reach what you paid." The kid looked at him. "Start at two sixty," Nolan said. "A dime makes two seventy. A quarter, two ninety-five. Another nickel, three dollars. Then the loonie, four dollars. Then the last loonie, five." The kid ran it with his finger moving along each coin, and when he landed exactly on five dollars, his whole face changed. "It's right," the kid announced, to nobody and everybody.

Nolan bought his milk, paid with a ten, and counted up his own change in his head the whole way to the door: seven eighty-five, then a dime, then quarters, then a toonie, then five, then ten. It landed exactly where it should. Outside, Spencer was still holding the bench down. Nolan held up the bag and the receipt.

"Everything there?" Spencer asked.

"Counted up from the price," Nolan said. "It's right."

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Snow looks white because its many clear ice crystals scatter and reflect all colors of light in every direction.
story:
Autumn had exactly one hour before Kasen and Georgia arrived with the sled, and her half-built snow fort looked like a pile of laundry. She patted another block into place, then stopped and stared at it. "You're white," she told the block. "But you're made of ice, and ice is clear." She held up a chunk of icicle she'd snapped off the porch railing, and she could see straight through it, sort of, like frosted glass in the dilapidated greenhouse next door.

The mystery bothered her so much that she carried the icicle inside, dripping, to ask her mom, who was hunting through the cupboard for Autumn's antibiotic for her ear. "Not now, honey, pharmacy run in ten minutes," her mom said. So Autumn carried the icicle back outside and turned it over and over, trying to perceive the difference between it and the snow.

When the sled crew showed up early, Georgia flopped into the unfinished fort and knocked a wall over. "Rude," Autumn said. "Also, question. This icicle is clear-ish. Snow is made of ice. Why is my whole yard white?"

Kasen squinted at the icicle, then scooped up a fistful of snow and held it next to the snowball. He looked like a boy doing math in his head. "Maybe it's like a shattered window," he said slowly. "One big piece of glass, you can see through. A thousand little pieces, all sparkly and bright, because every tiny piece bounces the light everywhere. Every which way. All the colors, at once."

"So all the colors bouncing back at you makes..." Autumn turned the snowball toward the gray sky. "White. Clear ice crystals, millions of them, all scattering light in every direction." She threw the snowball at Kasen's shoulder, purely for science. "That means every snowflake is basically a tiny mirror."

"That means you're standing in a yard full of broken windows," Georgia said, and began rebuilding the wall she'd wrecked. The three of them stacked blocks until the streetlights buzzed on, and the fort, white and glittering, finally looked like a castle made of light. "One more block," Autumn said, "and it's a drawbridge."

activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
knowledge_domain: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
fact: During a side breath in front crawl, skilled swimmers keep one goggle lens in the water and turn only far enough for the mouth to clear the surface.
story:
The park pool opened at ten, and by ten past Alexis was already failing. Twenty-five metres was only one length, but every time he breathed he lifted his whole face out of the water, and by the flags he felt like a sinking truck. Cedrik stood at the edge, eating chips he was supposedly saving for after. "You looked at the sky again," he said. "Both goggles out. Every single breath."

"I wasn't looking at the sky," Alexis said, coughing. "I was checking for birds." The water smelled of chlorine and hot concrete, and his left ear was full of it. He remembered last summer at the lake, watching his cousin glide past the dock, one lens of her goggles underwater, one eye on him like a shark that had decided to be friendly. She never seemed to slow down. He had never wondered why. He wondered now.

He pushed off again and ran a test. Test one: face straight up at the sky, like before. He counted his strokes to the flags and lost count of the splashing. Test two: turn only a little, just enough that his mouth broke the surface, one goggle lens still down in the water. It felt wrong, like reading a book sideways. But his legs stayed up and his arm kept reaching, and the flags arrived sooner than they ever had. He stopped at the wall, blinking. "Turn less," he told himself, as if reading instructions off the tile.

Cedrik offered him a chip as a jury of one delivered its verdict: "Faster." Ms. Morales, who coached the park swim club on Saturdays, was watching from the shallow end with her coffee. "Whatever you just changed," she called, "keep it." Alexis cherished that chip more than most trophies, and when his grandfather asked later why his old dog-paddle days now felt obsolete, Alexis only said, "I found out where the sky belongs." Then he grabbed his towel and ran back for one more length.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Looking at the horizon, a fixed distant point, can ease motion sickness because it helps the eyes agree with what the inner ear feels.
story:
The parking shuttle swayed around three corners before it finally stopped at the airport terminal, and by then Daniel's little sister had gone the color of old oatmeal. "I feel like a tsunami is happening inside my stomach," she mumbled, which was actually pretty funny, but Daniel knew better than to laugh. Their dad herded everyone toward the check-in counter while she clutched her paper bag like it was treasure.

While they waited in line, Daniel remembered something Ann had told him after her family's ferry trip last summer. She'd been queasy the whole crossing until she went up on deck and stared at the shoreline, and then her stomach had settled. "A fixed distant point," she'd said, waving her ice cream around. "The horizon. My eyes and my inner ear finally agreed about whether we were moving, and my stomach stopped arguing with everybody." At the time Daniel had thought it sounded like an excuse to eat ice cream, but now he had a hypothesis, and a queasy sister to test it on.

"Come on," he said, tugging her sleeve. "I want to try something. If it doesn't work, you can be mad at me for ten minutes." She complied, mostly because being mad took energy she didn't have. He walked her past the ticket machines to the huge glass wall at the end of the terminal, where the sky stretched out flat and wide above the runway. "Okay. Find the farthest thing you can see and don't look away." She frowned, then picked a point where the sky met the distant fields and stared at it like it owed her money.

They stood there for a while. A plane took off, and a man beside them started humming so badly that Daniel almost laughed, and his sister's frown cracked into a small grin, which was infectious. Then she blinked and said, "Hey. The tsunami is turning into, like, a regular small wave."

"Ann's horizon trick," Daniel announced to their dad when he came to find them, feeling like a scientist whose experiment had worked. "You're welcome." His sister rolled her eyes, but she kept her eyes on that far flat line all the way to their gate.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Many camps use a buddy system at the waterfront: each swimmer is paired with a partner, and at a 'buddy check' the pairs must find each other quickly so staff can count everyone.
story:
Rebecca's backpack was loaded for summer camp, three weeks at Lake Fernway, but today Mr. Wu had dragged her, Mahmoud, and a few neighbors onto the Ridge Trail for one last hike before the bus left on Saturday. "You'll be walking everywhere at camp," he said. "Get your boots used to it now."

Halfway up the switchbacks, Rebecca fell into step beside Mahmoud, who had spent last summer at Lake Fernway. She had been holding a worry all week, and the rhythm of the trail finally loosened it. "Can I confide something?" she asked. "I'm scared of the lake. Everybody swims twice a day, and I don't know how they keep track of so many kids in the water." Mahmoud picked up a stick and tapped the rocks as he walked. "They call it a buddy check," he said. "Every swimmer gets paired with a partner, and when the whistle blows, the pairs have to find each other fast so the staff can count everyone."

Rebecca turned that over for the next quarter mile. If her whole cabin lined up on the beach, the count would take forever; but if the counselors only had to count pairs, they could do it in seconds. Still, the system only worked if nobody wandered off, and Rebecca knew herself. She got distracted. She collected rocks. She followed frogs. "So if I chased a frog into the reeds," she said slowly, "my buddy couldn't raise her hand at the whistle, and they'd think someone drowned." Mahmoud grimaced. "That happened last year. A girl went off to look for her lost sandal, and her buddy was crying by the time the counselors found out. Everyone thought the worst."

Rebecca stopped on the trail to test the idea. "Okay, you're my buddy. Mr. Wu, can you whistle?" Mr. Wu, a few steps ahead, grinned and put two fingers in his mouth. The shrill note bounced off the ridge, and Rebecca spun around, hunting for Mahmoud's green cap among the pines. It took her only four seconds to spot him, but if he had drifted behind a boulder, she would have been lost, helpless, and worse, negligent toward a stranger who was counting on her. "I need a better plan than hoping," she said. "I'll tell my buddy on day one: if you lose me, look for cattails. I always end up near cattails." Mahmoud laughed and said that counted as the fairest negotiation he'd ever heard from a future camper.

They reached the overlook, where the valley opened up green and wide, and somewhere beyond the far ridge was a lake with a beach and a whistle. Rebecca pulled out the small compass her mother had packed and sighted along it, marking the direction. "Four days," she said, and clicked the compass shut.

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
knowledge_domain: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
fact: In MLA style, a prose quotation longer than four lines is set as an indented block, half an inch from the margin, without quotation marks.
story:
Noah had read "Where the Red Fern Grows" twice, and he knew exactly which passage proved that the theme was love that keeps going even after loss. The trouble was the quotation. He needed it for Monday's assignment, and his favourite part ran on and on, six lines on the page, too long to stuff into a sentence. He sat at his grandpa's kitchen table with the book open, a yellow pad, and a pencil he had already chewed.

His first try looked wrong the moment he wrote it. He had jammed the whole passage inside quotation marks, and it spilled across the page like a sentence that had eaten too much. His grandpa shuffled through with two mugs of cocoa and peeked over his shoulder. "That's a mighty long quote," he said. Noah agreed. Something about it had to change, but he didn't know what, and that was the real problem. He decided to simulate the finished page in his head, picturing what Ms. Moose wanted it to look like, and in the picture the quote stood alone, pushed inward from the edge. He just couldn't say why.

He texted Lilianna, who was doing the same assignment. She texted back fast: "mine was 5 lines, i looked it up." Then came a photo of the page in her handbook. Noah read it three times. In MLA style, a prose quotation longer than four lines is set as an indented block, half an inch from the margin, without quotation marks. So that was the rule. He erased his whole first attempt, which took stamina because his hand was tired and he wanted to quit, and started the paragraph again.

This time he introduced the quote in his own words first, naming the theme and saying where the moment happened in the story. Then he started a fresh line and indented it half an inch, using the width of his thumb as a rough measure. No quotation marks at all. The six lines sat in their own block, quiet and square, and underneath he wrote one more sentence tying the dogs' loyalty back to his claim. He read it over. It looked like a real page from a real paper.

"Read it to me," his grandpa said, settling into the chair across the table. Noah read the paragraph aloud, and when he finished, his grandpa was quiet for a second. "That holds together," he said. "You're resilient, boy. Most people would've quit after the erasing." Noah grinned and squared the pages, then slid the book into his backpack next to his pencil. "Monday, watch out," he said.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Prescription flu antiviral medicines work best when started within two days after symptoms begin, which is one reason to see a doctor early.
story:
Alicia sat at the kitchen table wrapped in a blanket that smelled like lemon tea, watching her dad's face turn a color she had only ever seen on a stop sign. Two days ago she had barely been able to lift her head off the couch, and now here he was, shivering by the kettle and insisting he was "fine, probably just tired."

"I think it's my turn," he joked weakly, but the thermometer disagreed. It read 39.2, which Alicia knew was high, because hers had read 38.9 and the doctor had made a small surprised face.

"The clinic's open until six," Alicia said. "You could go today."

Her dad waved a spoon at her. "It's Thursday. If I'm still bad on Saturday, I'll call. Viruses hibernate on weekends anyway, right?"

"They don't," Alicia said. "Nothing hibernates in you right now except maybe your good judgment." She was only half joking, but underneath the joke her brain was doing that thing it did, lining up facts like dominos. When she got sick, her mom had taken her to the doctor that same afternoon, and the doctor had prescribed an antiviral medicine for the flu. She remembered the exact words, because they had sounded like a deadline: these prescription flu medicines work best when you start them within two days after symptoms begin. Two days. Not Saturday. Thursday plus Saturday was three days, and three was more than two, and more than two was too late for the medicine to do its best work.

"Wait," she said, standing up so fast the blanket slid off. "My medicine. The doctor said it works best if you start it within two days after symptoms begin. You started symptoms this morning, right after you burned the toast and blamed the toaster. So if you wait until Saturday, you miss the window. That's why my doctor said one reason to see a doctor early."

Her dad blinked at her. "You were feverish and you remembered that?"

"I remember everything," Alicia said. "It's a neuron thing. Every single one of them was bored in that waiting room."

She dialed the clinic's number and held the phone out to him. He sighed, took it, and shuffled into the hallway, and she heard him say, "Yes, my daughter is making an excellent argument," which felt almost equivalent to winning a trophy.

While he was on the call, Thiago texted her the math homework, and Mr. Lee from next door knocked on the door with a pot of soup and the words "I heard sneezing through the wall." Alicia carried the soup to the stove, ladled two bowls, and set one at her dad's empty place at the table.

When he came back, he held up his car keys and said, "Appointment at five. The doctor asked who taught me about the two-day rule."

"Tell her it was the toast burner," Alicia said, and slid the bowl toward him.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats, and walks do not count as at-bats, so the number gives a batter no credit for walks.
story:
Romy stabbed a broccoli floret and held it up like evidence. "This is the third night in a row. I'm keeping data."

"Data is nutritious too," her dad said, sliding the casserole closer.

At school, the argument had been rattling around her head since lunch. Corbin had slammed his tablet on the table next to his tray and declared that his favorite player, a slugger named Diaz, was the most underrated hitter in the league, and that anyone who disagreed knew nothing about baseball. Sofie had glanced at the .247 batting average on the screen and laughed, which was maybe a bit of an embarrassment for Corbin, since half the cafeteria heard it. He had gone quiet, chewing his sandwich like it had personally wronged him, and said only, "It's not that simple."

Romy wanted to know what he meant. Not from politeness, exactly. She just could not stand a puzzle that sat unsolved, like a locked locker with the combination written somewhere she hadn't looked yet.

At dinner she pushed her plate aside and texted Sofie: ask Corbin tomorrow why it's not simple. Sofie replied with a single eye emoji, which meant yes. Meanwhile Romy pulled up box scores on her phone with one hand and ate rice with the other. She scrolled through Diaz's games. Hits, at-bats, hits, at-bats. Then she noticed a column she'd been skipping: walks. Diaz had a lot of them. Whole games where he never swung and still reached first base.

She did the division the way the stats page did it, hits divided by at-bats, and the walks sat there like guests who never got counted at the door.

The next day she found Corbin at his locker. "I figured out what you meant," she said. "Walks don't count as at-bats."

Corbin's face opened like a window. "Exactly! A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats, and walks aren't at-bats. Diaz gets on base constantly, and the number gives him zero credit for it."

"So .247 is hiding a whole other player," Sofie said, arriving with her backpack half unzipped.

Romy grinned. "I even wrote a rebuttal for whoever laughs next." She held up a napkin, covered in pencil numbers, and smoothed it flat on Corbin's locker door.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A fallen power line can still carry deadly electricity even when it is not sparking, so it should be treated as live, kept well away from, and reported.
story:
The lights at Grandpa's house went out just as Joshua was setting up his model bridge, and the whole living room dropped into the blue half-dark of early evening. Joshua found the flashlight in the kitchen drawer, the one Grandpa always kept in the same spot, and he heard the wind still shoving at the windows from the storm that had rolled through an hour before.

"The whole street's out," said Cayden, who had come over to work on the bridge too. He was peering between the curtains. "Every house I can see. Except the Hendersons', way down at the corner. Their porch light is still on."

Joshua stood beside him and looked. Their block curved, so the corner house sat where the wires crossed from the next street over. He tried to match each dark house to the line of poles outside, and the pattern seemed to correspond to which side of the road they were on. Every house on their side was black. "So it's not the whole street," he said slowly. "It's our section. Something's wrong between here and the corner."

Last summer, Joshua remembered, a storm had dropped a wire across the bike path behind the school, and Mackenzie had wanted to climb over it. He had grabbed her arm and pulled her back, and they had run to tell Mr. Grant, who had called it in. "A fallen power line can still carry deadly electricity even when it's not sparking," Mr. Grant had told the principal later, when Joshua was still standing there. "Treat it as live, keep well away, and report it." Joshua had never forgotten that, because it scared him how ordinary the wire had looked, just lying there like a jump rope.

Joshua was assertive about what they should do now. "We're not going near the poles. Grandpa, the power's out on our whole side of the block, and Cayden saw the Hendersons still have lights. There might be a line down somewhere between us and the corner." Grandpa counted the dark houses like he was taking a census, nodded, and called the power company from the hallway. Then he found the good lantern, and they all sat around the kitchen table while the bridge glue dried by lantern light.

Two trucks came eventually, their headlights sweeping the ceiling, and a man in heavy gear walked the sidewalk with a long pole, stopping near the corner where a limb had come down. Power hummed back on before the man left, and Grandpa went out to thank him. "Told you," Cayden said, holding up the finished bridge. Joshua grinned and set a stack of pennies on it, one by one.

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: Earth turns 15 degrees of longitude every hour, which is why time zones are roughly 15 degrees wide.
story:
Ethan pressed his finger against the giant world map on the wall of Ms. Thompson's Travel Agency, where his class had come on a field trip. He wanted to find the exact spot where his cousin had landed that morning, in Nairobi, and he only had a letter that said the city sat near latitude minus one and longitude thirty-seven east.

"Those lines are like an address," Camila said, tracing a horizontal line across the map with her own finger. "Latitude goes sideways, longitude goes up and down."

"Okay, so one degree south of the equator," Ethan said slowly, dragging his finger down until he found the line, then sliding it right until it crossed the other line near the east coast of Africa. "And thirty-seven east. Nairobi should be right there." He tapped the spot, and the city name sat half an inch away.

"Now the hard part," Lea said, holding up her phone. "My aunt wants to know what time to call them so she doesn't wake anybody up. It's ten in the morning here."

Ethan stared at the map. He remembered something odd his father had said before a business trip, that the reason for time zones was spinning around in his head all week. "Earth revolves," he said, "so the sun hits different places at different times." He counted the longitude lines between their city near ninety west and Nairobi near thirty-seven east. "That's about a hundred and twenty degrees. But how do I turn degrees into hours?"

Lea frowned. "Maybe it's one hour per ten degrees?"

"That's hypothetical," Ethan said. "Let's test it. When Dad flew to London, which is around zero longitude, he called us at ten at night and said it was five in the morning there. From ninety west to zero is ninety degrees." He counted on his fingers. "Ninety degrees, seven hours. That's not one per ten."

Camila grabbed a scrap of paper and started dividing. "Ninety divided by seven is almost thirteen. Hmm. What if the real rule is somewhere near fifteen degrees for every hour?"

Ethan did the math for Nairobi. One hundred twenty degrees divided by fifteen was eight hours ahead. He wrote the reasoning out in the margin of his notebook, checked it twice, and handed Lea the paper. "Tell your aunt to call at two in the afternoon. It'll be ten at night there, and people are still awake at ten."

Lea had been sure the answer was four hours. She read the paper, looked at the map, and shook her head. "I take it back. Two o'clock it is."

Ms. Thompson leaned over the counter with a grin and pointed at the wall of clocks above the brochures, each one labeled with a city. The Nairobi clock read exactly ten.

"Told you," Ethan whispered, and tapped the map one more time.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: In 1977, scientists in the submersible Alvin found deep-sea vent communities whose food chains start with bacteria using chemicals from the vents, not sunlight.
story:
The assignment sheet crumpled in Jace's fist as he knelt in the community garden beside a tomato vine. Draw a food chain, sun to top predator, and explain what happens if one link disappears. Easy, he thought, jabbing his pencil at the sky. Sun, tomato, caterpillar, bird. He had started to sketch the sun when Damon jogged up the gravel path with Louie's folded note in his hand.

"Read this before you get it wrong," Damon said, holding it out. Jace snatched it. Louie's messy handwriting read: "Skipped the garden. Watching a documentary for my chain. You're going to lose the bet. It doesn't start with the sun where these guys live. Ask Mr. Joseph about the year 1977." Jace's stomach tightened. The bet had been a bag of peaches from the fruit stand, and he had been so sure of the sun that he'd shaken on it.

He found Mr. Joseph turning compost behind the shed. Flashback: last summer, his grandfather, his first garden mentor, had shown him how to excavate a potato hill without slicing the tubers, and had said, "Nature follows rules, but rules have corners." So Jace asked, carefully, not about his homework, only whether every food chain truly began with sunlight. Mr. Joseph wiped his hands and told him the smallest thing, a sentence: "In 1977, scientists in the submersible Alvin found deep-sea vent communities whose food chains start with bacteria using chemicals from the vents, not sunlight." Then he went back to his shovel, offering nothing more.

Jace walked slowly back to the tomato vine, mind sprinting. Total darkness, miles down, and yet clams and crabs and stranger things lived there. So a chain could start with chemicals instead of light. He flipped his paper over and drew it: vent, bacteria, crab, something bigger with claws and no eyes. At the bottom he wrote what Louie would have to read out loud tomorrow: if the bacteria vanished, the whole chain would starve, link by link, all the way to the top. Damon leaned over his shoulder.

"You owe Louie peaches," Damon said.

"Probable," Jace admitted, and grinned as he drew the final arrow.

activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
knowledge_domain: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
fact: A closed contour loop with short tick marks pointing inward, called hachures, shows a hollow or depression rather than a hilltop.
story:
Autumn spread the topographic map across the library table just as Felipe slid into the chair beside her, still out of breath from biking. "The hike is tomorrow morning," he said. "Camilla's counting on us to pick the route, and I have to be home by five." The clock above the reference desk read 4:31.

"Then we have twenty-nine minutes to find the lookout," Autumn said. She traced her finger along the brown contour lines, the ones Mr. Choi had shown them when he handed over the maps from the library's drawer. "See how these lines bunch together on the west side? That's the steep slope, the fast way up." Camilla leaned in and nodded, tapping a small circle of contours near the summit. "That has to be the top. Closed loop, highest ground, best view. Let's pick that."

Something bothered Autumn, though. Around the inside edge of that closed loop, she noticed dozens of tiny marks, all pointing inward, like little eyelashes. Why would they point that way? She flipped through another map, then another, comparing hills she already knew. The hills had plain closed loops. Only this one had the tick marks. "Felipe," she said slowly, "what if this isn't a hill at all?" She remembered a trail guide she had abandoned on the cart by the window and darted over to fetch it. In the margin was a diagram just like her loop. "They're called hachures," she said, coming back. "A closed contour loop with short tick marks pointing inward, hachures, shows a hollow or depression, not a hilltop."

"So Camilla's lookout," Felipe said, "is a sunken pond?" Camilla laughed, redrew the route along the western ridgeline, and marched up to Mr. Choi's desk to have it checked. He ran one finger down the contour lines, glanced at his watch, and stamped the map. "Good catch," he said. "Now go, before I lock the doors and make you two my official map ambassadors forever." Camilla grabbed her backpack and held the door while the daylight poured in.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Chocolate contains theobromine, which dogs break down very slowly, and dark or baking chocolate is far more dangerous to them than milk chocolate.
story:
Nathaniel stood in front of the puppy pen at the pet store, trying to choose. Ms. Cohen, who owned the shop, had told him three were left, and he had narrowed it down to two. The little brown one with white paws kept pressing her nose against the glass whenever he leaned close, and the spotted one just watched. "You already picked, haven't you," said Natalie, who had come along to carry the bag of supplies. She was right. He asked Ms. Cohen for the brown one, and she lifted the puppy out with both hands and set her in his arms, warm and trembling.

While Ms. Cohen filled out the paperwork, she talked through the basics: food, water, a crate, patience. Then she pointed at a shelf of treats and said one thing firmly. "No chocolate, ever. It has something in it called theobromine, and dogs break it down very slowly." She added that dark or baking chocolate was far more dangerous to them than milk chocolate, and that a small dog needed only a little to get sick. Nathaniel nodded, but half of his attention was on the puppy chewing the string of his hoodie.

At home, he set up the crate in the kitchen and named her Mika, after his friend Mika who moved away last spring, because she had the same steady, watchful look. For two days everything went fine. On the third afternoon, his mother set a bag of baking chocolate on the counter, and while Nathaniel answered the door for Natalie, the puppy found a chair, then the counter, then the bag. They came back to shredded paper and dark crumbs on the floor.

Nathaniel's stomach dropped, but he made himself think instead of panic. A whole bag, and it was baking chocolate. He remembered the comparison, that dark chocolate was worse than milk, so a small amount of this could matter a lot for a small puppy. Guilt might have hindered him, making him want to hide the mess, but he pushed that aside and called the vet's office, because calling was the only legitimate thing to do. The nurse on the phone asked what kind and how much. "Baking chocolate," he said. "Most of a bag." She told him to bring Mika in right away.

An hour later he sat in the waiting room with Mika wrapped in a towel on his lap. Natalie had followed on her bike and now sat beside him, quiet for once. When the vet tech finally opened the door and said Mika would be fine, that they had caught it in time, Nathaniel let out a long breath. Mika lifted her head and licked his wrist once. "No more counters," he told her. "Ever."

activity: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them
knowledge_domain: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them
fact: A sprint hurdler leans the chest forward over the lead leg while clearing a hurdle, so the body keeps moving forward instead of rising up.
story:
Zack lined up the five low hurdles across the backyard grass, spacing them at his best guess, which was an approximate distance because he was measuring with his sneakers, not a tape measure. Samson stood by the fence holding a stopwatch and a juice box. Ziyad sat on the porch steps eating crackers like a civilian at a sporting event, which he announced he was.

"Three steps between hurdles," Zack said. "That's the rhythm. One-two-three, hop." He sprinted at the first hurdle, took off, and sailed over it sitting almost upright, like a kid on a very fast swing. He landed heavy, stuttered, took five steps to the next hurdle, clattered it with his knee, and ended up tangled in hurdle number three while the fourth and fifth stood there untouched, smug about it.

"You looked like a parachute," Samson said, checking the watch. "You went up and then you had to come back down before you could run again."

Zack walked back to the start, chewing on that. He hadn't thought about up and down at all. He had been thinking only about getting over. He watched the problem in his mind: if he jumped up high, he had to wait to come down, and waiting killed the one-two-three. So maybe the answer was to stop going up so much. He tried again, this time pushing his chest forward over his lead leg as he cleared the hurdle instead of rising tall over it. One-two-three, hurdle. One-two-three, hurdle. He clipped the fourth one but ran through, and crossed the last hurdle still moving, breathless and grinning.

"Do that again," Samson said. "I want to demonstrate it to the track coach. Also I wasn't watching the time, I was drinking juice."

From next door, Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya leaned over the fence with her watering can. "Whatever that was," she called, "it looked smoother than the parachute attempt."

"That was the old model," Ziyad said, bowing from the steps. "This is the new and improved Zack."

Zack jogged back to the start, set his feet, and said, "Watch the chest this time."

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: A null hypothesis is the statement that there is no relationship between the things being studied, which an experiment then tries to reject.
story:
The basil on the windowsill had two leaves left, and Evan meant to keep it alive. "For the science fair," he said, spreading three seed packets across the kitchen table while his friend Karim dumped soil into paper cups. "Ms. Zhou says we need a real experiment, not just a display." Karim wanted the blue ribbon more than anything, because his older brother had won it twice, so he leaned over the handout and read aloud until he hit a problem. "It says we have to state the null hypothesis. Do you know what that is?" Evan shook his head, and neither of them wanted to ask, because Ms. Zhou had already explained it once and they had been too busy arguing about speakers.

They planted twelve seeds, six for the music group and six for the quiet group, and labeled every cup. "I think the music ones will grow taller," Evan said. "So if we're right, the quiet ones have to stay behind." Karim frowned at the word on the handout again, then snapped his fingers. "It's called the null hypothesis," he said. "It's the statement that there's no relationship between the things you're studying, and the experiment tries to reject it." Evan wrote it at the top of their data sheet in careful letters. Their rule: if the music cups and quiet cups grew about the same, the experiment would fail to reject it, and their guess would be sunk.

Every morning before school, Evan played his trumpet softly at one tray while the other tray sat tranquil in the corner. He kept a notebook, and Karim acquired the job of measuring, since his hands were steadier with the ruler. They measured in millimeters and argued about whether a sprout counted at two millimeters or three. "It counts when I can see it without squinting," Karim said, and Evan wrote that rule down too.

After two weeks the results looked like a tie, and Karim slumped at the table. Then Evan noticed something. The quiet tray sat farther from the window, and the sun shifted toward the music cups all afternoon. "We can't say anything about music," he said slowly, "because the light wasn't fair." They moved the trays, started a second run, and Karim grinned as he flipped to a clean page. "Good thing we bought extra seeds."

activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
knowledge_domain: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
fact: On U.S. Geological Survey topographic maps, contour lines are printed in brown.
story:
Camille pressed her nose against the window of Baxter's Travel Agency, where a giant map of the Pine Ridge hiking area hung behind the counter, covered in thin brown squiggles. She was supposed to pick a hiking route for her class trip, and Mr. Mehta had said, "Choose wisely, because the trail you pick is the one we all climb." The problem was that she had no idea which trail was steep and which was gentle, and last year a boy named Dominic had picked a route that left everyone's legs shaking for two days.

Inside, the shop smelled of coffee and old paper. Angelique was already there, sliding brochures across the counter toward a woman behind the register. "My dad says if I can get people to book the waterfall tour, the extra revenue might convince him to let me come along as a junior guide," Angelique said, arranging the brochures so the shiniest ones sat on top. "But the waterfall trail is the one nobody can figure out. It looks flat on the little map."

Camille looked up at the big map on the wall. All those brown lines, bunched together in some places and spread far apart in others. She remembered the folded map at home, the one her mother had used at the lake, and how she'd once traced a brown line with her finger and wondered what it was. She traced one now, following it across the hillside like a tiny road. "These brown lines," she said slowly, "I think they show the shape of the ground. The land is the same height all along each line."

"That's contour lines," Angelique said, reading the tiny legend at the bottom of the map. "It says so right here."

Camille's heart jumped. She spread her fingers where the brown lines crowded together near the waterfall, like spaghetti pushed to one side of the pot, and then where they drifted apart on the far slope. If the lines meant height, then lines close together must mean the ground was rising fast, all that height squeezed into a short distance. Lines far apart would mean a slow, easy climb. She grabbed a pencil and made a small X on the gentle slope, then tested her idea by checking the elevations printed along the trails. The far slope climbed only two hundred feet. The spaghetti section climbed more than twice that, in half the distance.

She articulated her finding to the woman at the register, pointing at the tight brown cluster. "That's the steepest part, so the trail should switch back over here instead." The woman raised her eyebrows and pulled out a trail guide, and there it was in print, a proposed reroute around the exact spot Camille had marked.

"Two waterfall bookings," Angelique announced a few minutes later, holding up slips of paper with a buoyant grin. "Because I told them it's the easy way up now." Camille folded her copy of the route into her pocket and headed for the door, already planning to show Mr. Mehta the brown lines first thing Monday.

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: In rock-paper-scissors, each choice beats exactly one other choice and loses to exactly one, so no choice is better than the others.
story:
Megan pushed her peas around her plate while her dad asked the usual dinner questions, and she finally said, "Landon says rock always wins."

Her mom laughed. "That's a plague that goes back generations. Your uncle insisted the same thing when he was ten."

"It's not funny," Megan said. "Zia picked rock for the tetherball line, and Landon picked rock too, and then Landon said his rock was stronger because he threw it harder, so he got the spot. Zia said that wasn't fair, and then they both got mad at me because I didn't take a side." She could still picture Zia's face going red, the way her voice climbed an octave, and how Landon had folded his arms like a wall. At the time Megan had just shrugged and said "whatever," and then walked to the back of the line. She kept thinking about that shrug all through math.

"Did you say anything to Mr. Han?" her dad asked.

"He was on yard duty at the far fence. By the time he came over it was already a shouting match." Megan put down her fork. "Tomorrow we're doing the dispute again because Zia wants a rematch, and Landon says he'll just win again."

Her little brother, who was seven and mostly ate with his face, held up a fist, a flat hand, and two fingers. "Rock, paper, scissors."

Megan stared at him. She had never actually mapped it out before. She set down her fork and made the shapes herself, one after another, under the kitchen light. "Wait," she said slowly. "Rock loses to paper. Paper loses to scissors. And scissors lose to rock." She tried to find a shape that beat everything, or lost to everything, and she couldn't. Each one beat exactly one other and lost to exactly one. "None of them is better. It's even all the way around."

"So Landon's rock isn't stronger?" her mom asked.

"It can't be. It's just even." Megan felt something click into place, the same click she got when a math problem stopped being a wall and became a door. She ran upstairs, found a notebook, and wrote three lines: the problem, the rule, and what she would say. Landon couldn't articulate it, probably, but she could.

The next day at lunch she stood between Zia and Landon before the arguing could start. "Here's the problem," she said, keeping her voice level the way her mom did during jury calls. "Landon thinks rock wins. It doesn't. Rock beats scissors and loses to paper, paper loses to scissors, scissors lose to rock. Everything's even. So here's the rule. We throw it once, fair, and nobody gets to say 'harder.' Deal?"

Zia said deal right away. Landon narrowed his eyes, then nodded.

They threw. Zia's paper wrapped Landon's rock, and Zia jogged to the front of the line, pumping her fist.

"Best two out of three?" Landon called after her.

"Next time," Megan said, and held up two fingers, snipping the air.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Gleaning is an ancient practice: the Book of Leviticus in the Hebrew Bible tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested for the poor and for strangers.
story:
Tyler pushed through the door marked ANIMAL SHELTER and stopped dead. Instead of barking and the smell of kibble, he found folding tables stacked with canned soup, pasta and peanut butter, and a line of people already forming outside. A woman with a clipboard explained that the shelter shared the building with the community food bank, and that the volunteer sign-up sheets had gotten mixed up. His Saturday with the dogs was actually a Saturday here. He tried not to let his shoulders slump too obviously, because the line outside was getting longer and nobody had time for his disappointment.

He was put at the sorting table with Gemma and a kid named Eshal, whose grandmother had come along to help. A crate of slightly dented cans sat under the table, separate from the rest, with a handwritten label that just said GLEANING. "Why do the weird cans get their own word?" Tyler asked. Nobody knew. Eshal's grandmother squinted at the label and smiled. "My mother would have known that word," she said. "Gleaning, it's an ancient practice. The Book of Leviticus in the Hebrew Bible tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested, for the poor and for strangers." She said it the way you'd remind someone of a song lyric, then went back to taping boxes.

Tyler turned that over while he sorted. A rule where you don't take everything, he thought. You leave the edges. He watched the front tables, where volunteers handed out bags, and noticed a pattern: the families who arrived last, right before closing, got whatever was left, which was often the least. On the wall behind him hung a poster of an endangered tortoise the shelter was helping, which reminded him that small, careful efforts were supposed to matter. He had an idea, and he decided to test it.

"We should put the gleaning crate up front," he told Gemma, "but not open it until the last hour. Like an edge of the field nobody harvests early." The clipboard woman agreed to let them try it, so Tyler set the crate on the end table and settled in to monitor it from his sorting station, glancing over every few minutes. Eshal kept a tally of how many families came after four o'clock; the percentage was small, maybe one in ten, but those were exactly the families whose bags had been thinnest.

At five to five, a man with two kids picked through the gleaning crate and found the dented cans of chili, the good ones nobody had claimed because their labels were torn. "These are perfect," he said, loading his bag. He looked at Tyler and added, "You saved the best for last." Across the hall, a dog barked once, as if agreeing. Tyler went to fetch another crate for next Saturday, both of them, shelter and food bank, on the same sign-up sheet.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Stress is the body's response to a demand or challenge, and short bursts of it can help a person focus, such as before a test or a race.
story:
Nolan arrived at Harlyn's house with a bag of gummy worms, because Harlyn had a piano recital in three hours and had texted him one word: HELP. He found her sitting at the kitchen table, staring at her sheet music like it might stare back. Her little brother was drumming on the counter with two wooden spoons, which did not seem to be helping.

"I can't do it," Harlyn said. "My hands get sweaty, my stomach hurts, and my anxiety makes everything worse. Maybe I'll fake a fever." She coughed in a way that fooled nobody, not even the dog.

Nolan chewed a gummy worm and thought. Last month he'd been so nervous before the spelling bee that his stomach had hurt too, and he'd spelled every word right, even "luminous," which means glowing. His hands had been steady on the buzzer the whole time. That was weird. The nerves had felt awful but his brain had worked better, not worse. He turned a spoon around and drew a little test on a napkin: a list, like a hierarchy, from "not nervous at all" up to "sick with worry," and he put a star in the middle. "Here's my idea," he said. "I think the middle is the sweet spot."

"Explain," said Harlyn, who was taking bites out of a slice of bread with no filling, which was her coping method, along with pacing.

"Stress is your body's response to a demand or challenge," Nolan said, "and short bursts of it can actually help you focus, like before a test or a race. So your sweaty hands might be your body getting ready, not breaking." He slid the napkin across the table. "Let's test it. Play the piece once while totally relaxed, and once while a little scared. Then compare."

Harlyn went to the piano. The first time, her brother drummed along gently and she flopped through the music like a sock puppet. Then Nolan modified the experiment: he set the kitchen timer for two minutes and said if she hit a wrong note, the timer would buzz and she'd have to start over, and also he would eat one of her gummy worms. Her eyes narrowed. She sat up, set her shoulders, and played the whole piece clean, and when the timer buzzed at the end she was still playing the last chord.

"Okay," she said slowly. "That was better. That was a lot better."

At the recital that evening, Harlyn's hands were sweating and her stomach was doing its usual thing, and she played with her eyes narrowed, like she did when gummy worms were at stake. Afterward she bowed, then marched straight over to Nolan's seat. "I'm keeping the napkin," she said. "Give me the napkin."

activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
knowledge_domain: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
fact: The rule of 72 estimates how many years money takes to double: divide 72 by the yearly interest rate, so at 24 percent, about three years.
story:
Joseph stood in aisle four of Martino's Grocery, holding two boxes of the same cereal, one big and one small, doing math in his head. Masen had bet him a dollar that the big box was always cheaper per ounce, and Joseph was proving him wrong when Mr. Shapiro came around the corner with his little hand basket.

"Unit prices," Mr. Shapiro said, tapping the yellow sticker on the shelf. "Your grandmother teach you that?" Joseph nodded. His grandmother was why he was here at all. Last night she had shown him a credit card statement from years ago, back when she was saving for his mom's college, and she had sighed and said, "I should have postponed some purchases instead." Joseph hadn't understood what she meant, so today he was watching how money actually moved, starting with cereal.

Masen found them a minute later and slapped his dollar into Joseph's palm. "Fine, the small box wins. You're a human calculator." Then he pulled out his phone and showed Joseph a glossy ad for a gaming headset, one hundred eighty dollars, no money down if you used a store card. "My cousin got one this way. You just pay later."

Joseph did not say anything right away. He was thinking about the statement from last night, the part where the balance had grown even though his grandmother wasn't buying anything new. He remembered the interest rate printed at the top: 24 percent. He had looked it up after bedtime and found something called the rule of 72. He tested it now, quietly, in aisle four. "Seventy-two divided by 24 is 3," he said to Masen. "So money doubles in about three years at that rate." Masen blinked. "What money?"

"That's the thing. It's invisible. If you owe one eighty on a card at 24 percent and don't pay it, the rule of 72 says it turns into about three sixty in three years. You'd pay for two headsets and own one." Joseph set the cereal in the cart. "My grandma's balance doubled like that. That's what she meant about postponing."

Masen squinted at the ad like it had turned into a snake. "My cousin said it was free money." They walked toward the registers, and Joseph felt a little heavy, wondering whether telling Masen made him a good friend or a boring one. Last summer he had begged his mom for a fifty dollar game and she had said no, and he had sulked for days. Now the memory sat differently, like a puzzle piece that had finally found its edge.

At the register, the cashier rang up the groceries, and Joseph counted out the exact cash his grandmother had given him, watching the total shrink to zero with a clean, final beep. Then Mr. Shapiro appeared beside them, set down his basket, and slid a folded sheet of paper across the counter to Joseph. "Your grandmother asked me to give you this." Joseph opened it. It was a savings account statement, his name on it, a deposit of one hundred eighty dollars, and a note in her handwriting: the equivalent of Masen's headset, sitting there earning interest instead of owing it. Joseph looked up, and Mr. Shapiro just smiled and picked up his bag.

"Three years," Joseph said, folding the paper back along its crease.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: When the price of one good rises, many buyers switch to a substitute, a similar good that does the same job, so demand for the substitute goes up.
story:
Payton pushed the cart straight toward aisle six, because Saturday meant movie night, and movie night meant popcorn, the good kind with the blue mountain on the bag. But when she reached the shelf, the tag stopped her cold. Five dollars and eighty cents. Last week it had been three fifty. Behind her, Mabel gasped like they'd discovered treasure, except it was the opposite of treasure.

"That can't be right," Payton said. She picked up a bag anyway, turned it over, and put it back. "It's the same popcorn. Same bag, same mountain."

"Maybe there wasn't much popcorn grown this year," Mabel said. "My grandpa says that happens with things, when there isn't much of something and everybody wants it, the price climbs." She pointed at the shelf, where only four bags sat in a space that could hold twenty. "See? Almost gone. It's like a siege on the popcorn."

Payton stared at the empty space. Then her eyes slid one shelf down, where another brand sat in tall, full rows: same size bag, plain red label, two dollars and seventy cents. She grabbed one and held them side by side. "This one does the same job. It pops, it's salty, it's buttery enough." She dropped the red bag into the cart. "And if everybody else does what we just did, watch."

They wheeled around the end of the aisle and nearly crashed into Theodor, who was clutching a red bag of the exact same popcorn. "The blue kind went up to almost six dollars," he said, holding it out like evidence. "My mom sent me to get the cheap one instead. Everybody at the checkout has these."

Payton's grin felt almost too big for her face. "I said that would happen! Not the exact part about you, but the switching part." She counted the red bags in other carts as they rolled toward the front. Two. Four. Seven. Meanwhile the blue bags just sat there, expensive and alone.

At the checkout, Mr. Sandhu from next door was ahead of them, and of course he had a red bag too. "I'll demonstrate my theory," Payton announced, pointing at his cart. "Blue price goes up, so people switch to the similar one, and now everyone wants the red kind instead. That's why the shelf is emptying down there and full up here."

Mr. Sandhu laughed. "You should teach a class." He paid, gathered his bags, and headed for the door.

The cashier scanned the red popcorn and paused. "Funny thing," she said. "We sold more of these today than we usually sell in a week. I'll have to call in an order." Payton leaned on the cart and whispered to Mabel, "And if it gets scarce enough, guess what happens to its price next."

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: The law of supply says that when the price of something rises, sellers offer more of it, because producing it becomes more profitable.
story:
