Dominic's grandfather kept a jar of coins on the shelf beside the strawberry jam, and every Saturday they walked to the market together. This Saturday, Dominic stared at the chalkboard behind the berry stand. Four dollars a basket. Last month it had been two.

"Grandpa, why so high?" he asked.

"Frost took half the crop," Grandpa said, patting the jar in his coat pocket. "Fewer berries, higher price. That part you know."

But it was the next Saturday that made Dominic stop in the middle of the lane. Where one berry stand had stood, there were now four. New tables, new hand-painted signs, baskets stacked in red pyramids. The air smelled of crushed fruit and rain-damp wood.

"Joanna," he said, grabbing his friend's sleeve, "count the stands."

"Four," said Joanna, chewing a berry she'd bought with her own coins. "So? Strawberries are good."

Dominic pulled out the little notebook he kept in his back pocket, the one with a broken constitution that made its pages flap loose in the wind. He pressed them flat against the table. "Hypothetical," he said slowly. "Say I'm a farmer. Say strawberries go from two dollars to four dollars. Suddenly I'd make more money off every basket, right? So maybe I'd plant more. Or maybe people who never sold berries before would start."

"Meaning what?" Joanna asked.

"Selling them becomes more profitable. That's what the price signifies to a seller. So when the price rises, sellers offer more of them. It's like a rule." He tapped the notebook. "The price didn't just tell buyers to be careful. It told growers to show up."

At the fourth stand, a woman Dominic had never seen handed him a basket. "First week selling," she admitted. "Saw what berries were going for."

Dominic grinned and counted out four dollars. "One more question," he said. "What happens if everybody plants strawberries next year?"

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Psychologist Thomas Gordon coined the term 'I-message' in the 1960s: a sentence like 'I felt left out' describes the speaker's feelings instead of blaming the listener with 'you'.
story:
The trouble started on Tuesday, when Madeleine walked off the swings with Jerome and didn't look back. Samantha sat alone on the woodchips, holding the two blue jacks she'd been saving for their game. On Wednesday Madeeline ate lunch with Jerome's table, and on Thursday she did it again, laughing at something Samantha couldn't hear.

By Friday Samantha had a plan, and the plan was a sentence. She worked on it in her notebook during silent reading, out of sight of Mr. Tang. Her first try was "You ditched me at recess," but when she read it back it sounded like an accusation, the kind of sentence that made people cross their arms. She remembered Mr. Tang saying once, while handing back their conflict-resolution worksheets, that a psychologist named Thomas Gordon coined the term "I-message" back in the 1960s. She'd looked it up afterward: a sentence like "I felt left out" describes the speaker's own feelings instead of blaming the listener with "you." She crossed out her first line and wrote, "I felt left out when you went to Jerome's table." Then she folded the paper twice and put it in her pocket, because recess was in ten minutes.

At recess, a wedge of migratory geese passed overhead, honking their way south in a long ragged V. Samantha watched them until her neck ached. The class had voted that morning by ballot on which game to buy for indoor days, and Madeleine had counted the votes without looking up once. That was the detail that convinced Samantha the whole thing wasn't an accident, because Madeleine always narrated the counting, every single raised hand.

Samantha found Madeeline by the fence, tying her shoe. Her heart was going fast, but she had decided that the note was something she could conquer, like the high dive at the pool, and the trick was the same: don't stop at the edge. She held out the folded paper.

"I wrote something," she said. "You can read it or I can say it."

Madeeline straightened up. She took the paper, unfolded it, and read. Her shoulders came down slowly, like she'd been carrying something too.

"I didn't know you felt that way," Madeleine said. "Jerome said you were mad at me because I beat you at four square, so I figured you wanted space. I was going to give you until Monday."

"That's not what happened at all," Samantha said, almost laughing.

"Obviously not now." Madeeline pulled two blue jacks out of her coat pocket. "I kept these. Want to play?"

The geese called once more from far overhead, and Samantha sat down on the woodchips beside her friend.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: The placebo effect is when people feel better after a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill, simply because they expect it to help.
story:
Grandpa arrived at the reunion carrying a bright orange tin decorated with a logo Alexander recognized from television ads. "Zest Corporation's finest," Grandpa announced, holding it up like a trophy. "One mug of this every morning, and my cold was gone in two days." The tin depicted a sunrise over a mountain range, and beneath it, in bold letters, the words FEEL BETTER, NATURALLY.

Alexander stirred his lemonade and thought about what had happened in Ms. Esposito's science class back in October. She had given one group real medicine for headaches and another group sugar pills, and the sugar pill group reported feeling better too, just because they expected to. "That's called the placebo effect," she had said, and then made them design their own simple tests. Alexander's first attempt had been a mess, half-finished and confusing, and Myriam had helped him redo it until his chart was coherent enough to read at a glance. He had learned that a single person's story, even a true one, wasn't the same as a claim backed by a test.

His cousin Maude was sitting across the picnic table, sniffling into a napkin. "I feel awful," she mumbled. Alexander grabbed two plain mugs from the serving table, filled both with ordinary peppermint tea from the big pot, and dropped a plain tea bag into each. Then he slid one toward Maude. "This one's from the fancy tin," he said, keeping his face as straight as he could. Myriam, who was passing the potato salad, raised an eyebrow but played along. "Oh, the mountain sunrise blend," she said. "Premium."

Maude sipped, sighed, and twenty minutes later declared that her head felt clearer. "That stuff really works," she said. Alexander held up the second mug, identical down to the last drop. "This one's exactly the same," he said, "plain tea from the pot. You just expected the fancy one to help." Maude blinked at him, then at the mug, then back at him.

"Wait," she said. "Do that again, but this time don't tell me which is which."

Alexander was already boiling the kettle.

activity: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
knowledge_domain: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
fact: A Scratch variable made 'for all sprites' can be used by every sprite, while one made 'for this sprite only' belongs to a single sprite.
story:
The gymnasium was supposed to be tranquil before a robotics competition, but by eight in the morning it was already humming with laptops and nerves. Joshua unrolled his mouse pad beside his project, a Scratch game where a cat caught falling coins, and waited for the judges to call his table. He had enrolled in the competition back in September mostly because Candice dared him to, and now here he was, with a game that almost worked.

Almost was the problem. When the cat touched a coin, the score was supposed to go up by one, and when a coin hit the ground, it was supposed to drop by one. The gaining worked. The losing did not. "Watch," Joshua said to Guneet, who had wandered over from her own table. He ran the game, steered the cat under three coins, and the score climbed to three. Then he let a coin fall past the cat and splat onto the grass. The score stayed at three.

"Maybe the coin's script isn't even running," Guneet said. Joshua shook his head, because he had put a speech bubble in it, and when the coin landed, the words "missed me" popped up just fine. So the script ran, the block sat right there, change score by negative one, and nothing happened. What could stop a block that was definitely running? He sat back and wondered about that, tapping his pencil. The coin could talk. The coin could fall. The coin just couldn't touch the score.

Then he noticed something he had never really looked at. When he made the score inside the cat's script, a little window had asked him a question, and he had clicked through it fast, the way he did at home when he wanted leisure and not menus. He opened the Variables category and stared. There were two score variables listed, not one. Two. "Wait," he said slowly. "I made one for the cat, and the coin made its own." Guneet leaned in. "For this sprite only," she read off the first one, "and this one says for all sprites."

Joshua dragged the cat's score into the trash and kept the one marked for all sprites. He rebuilt the cat's scoring loop, then the coin's if-then block, touching edge, change score by negative one. He started the game, caught two coins, missed one on purpose, and watched the number go two, two, one. He grabbed Guneet's sleeve. "One," she said. "Look at that. It went down." Across the gym, Ms. Pham called, "Table six, two minutes," and Joshua hit the green flag one more time, just to see it happen again.

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: Metals such as copper conduct electricity well, while plastic and rubber are insulators, which is why wires are copper covered in plastic.
story:
Brooklyn had twenty minutes before Ms. Szabó's circuit demonstration, and the bulb would not light. She had the battery, the switch, the bulb, and two wires, and she had clipped everything together exactly the way the diagram showed, twice. Nothing. Megan leaned over her shoulder with the smug patience of someone whose bulb was already glowing on the next desk.

"Maybe your battery's dead," Megan offered.

"It's not dead, it's brand new." Brooklyn frowned at the setup. Something was missing, but it was missing somewhere she couldn't see. Electricity was like that, invisible until it worked or didn't. She flipped the switch again, as though the third attempt might be charmed.

Then she remembered the earbuds. Last summer her cousin's dog had chewed the cord, and Brooklyn had seen the inside: beneath the grey plastic, a twist of shiny copper, bright as a new penny. Copper, inside plastic. She picked up one of her clip wires and studied the end. It was copper-colored on the outside, but when she scratched it with her thumbnail, a thin pale layer peeled away, and underneath was real metal, gleaming. The plastic was coating it, all along the part that was supposed to touch the clips.

"You've got a monopoly on the not-working circuits," said Lana from across the table, holding up her own glowing bulb like a trophy.

"I've got a predatory streak," Brooklyn muttered. "Just watch." She borrowed the wire stripper from the supply drawer and, remembering how careful she'd been with the earbuds, stripped a centimeter of plastic off each end of both wires. Bare copper stuck out, bright and clean. She clipped the metal parts tight to the battery, the switch, and the bulb, checked that every join was copper touching copper, and closed the switch.

The bulb lit. Warm yellow, steady, smug right back at Lana.

"How'd you fix it?" Megan asked, leaning in.

"The plastic was blocking everything. Metals like copper conduct electricity really well. Plastic and rubber are insulators. That's why the wires are copper covered in plastic, I guess, so the plastic keeps it where it belongs and the copper does the actual work."

Ms. Szabó paused at their table on her rounds. "Show the class in ten minutes, Brooklyn. You're first."

Brooklyn raised her hand anyway. "Can I strip one more wire? I want them to see the shiny part."

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: Transition words such as first, however, furthermore and therefore link paragraphs and show the reader how one idea relates to the next.
story:
The essay was due on Friday, and Declan had written it three times already, but it still sounded like five separate assignments stapled together. His topic was solid: the school should replace its ancient, broken chess boards, and it should not let one company have a monopoly on supplying the new ones. He had evidence. He had even made Omer count the missing pawns with him after class, seventeen in total. What he did not have was flow.

He spread the pages across the small table at the corner of Mr. Jung's cafe, where the wifi was free and Mr. Jung was indifferent to students who ordered one hot chocolate and stayed for two hours. Omer slid into the other chair and picked up the essay.

"Listen to this," Omer said, and read the start of each paragraph out loud in a flat robot voice. "The school needs new chess boards. The old boards are damaged. One supplier is a problem. Buy from several companies. New boards will help everyone."

Declan winced. "That bad, huh?"

"It's like the paragraphs aren't even talking to each other." Omer tapped the page. "When you talk, you don't just jump. You say stuff like 'but' and 'so.' "

Declan stared at the essay. That was it, maybe. The paragraphs weren't jumping randomly; they were steps in an argument, and he had left out the handrails. He pulled out a pencil and wrote a single word at the top of the second paragraph: "First," the old boards were damaged. Then, before the paragraph about the supplier, he wrote "However," one supplier was a problem, because the reader needed to know he was shifting direction, not just piling on. He tried a third one. "Furthermore," buying from several companies would cost less. And at the end, right before the conclusion, he added "Therefore," the school should act now.

He slid the pages back to Omer. "Read it again. Same robot voice."

Omer read, and halfway through the robot voice turned back into a normal voice without either of them deciding it should. He stopped and grinned. "It's one essay now. It's like the words walk the reader across."

Declan looked at his five paragraphs, which had somehow become one argument. There was still work to do; he needed to cite the interview he had done with the chess coach in the third paragraph, and his conclusion was basically his introduction wearing a hat. But the bones worked.

Mr. Jung came over with a plate of day-old muffins and set it down without a word. Declan took one, licked a crumb of pencil graphite off his thumb, and started writing his conclusion. "Therefore," he said out loud as he wrote it, "the very first thing Mr. Ruiz should do is open the supply order to everyone."

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: The Gunnery camp, begun in 1861 by Connecticut schoolmaster Frederick W. Gunn, who led his students on a hike to a camp by the sea, is usually considered the first organized American summer camp.
story:
Peyton sat at the far end of the lakeside dock with her duffel bag between her knees, watching the camp van bump down the gravel road on the other side of the water. She had one hour before it came for her, and she was spending it the way she'd spent the whole week, pretending she wasn't scared.

"You're going to be the only first-timer," Nola had said back in June, on the last day of school. Peyton could still see her standing by the classroom door, backpack over one shoulder. "Everybody else went last year. They'll have inside jokes and secret handshakes, and you'll be the new kid who can't paddle." Peyton had said something neutral, like "probably," but the words had stuck to her all summer like burrs on a sock.

Now she stared at the dark water and thought about it like a math problem. If everyone already knew each other, then the first week would be awful, and the second week would be worse, because by then the groups would be set. That was the rule of fifth grade, and she assumed it was the rule everywhere. But maybe it wasn't. Rules could be local, like how you had to take your shoes off at Nola's house but not at Emmett's. Peyton looked around the dock for a way to test the idea, and spotted a wooden plaque bolted to the post by the boat rack. She walked over and read it.

The plaque said the dock and the camp had a history. A Connecticut schoolmaster named Frederick W. Gunn had begun the Gunnery camp in 1861, leading his students on a hike to a camp by the sea, and that camp was usually considered the first organized American summer camp. Peyton read it twice. 1861. That was during the Civil War, back when people traveled by horse. Summer camp wasn't some thing invented last decade for kids with inside jokes. It was old, and if it was that old, then every camper in history had once been a first-timer. Even Frederick W. Gunn's students, hiking to the sea, had been first-timers on that trail. The test of her rule had failed, which meant the rule itself might be wrong.

"You're Peyton, right?" A woman in a staff shirt was walking down the dock, checking a clipboard. "I'm Ms. Tremblay, I monitor the bus loading. Van's early, I'm afraid." Peyton hoisted her duffel, then paused and pointed at the plaque. "Did you know this camp stuff started in 1861? A schoolmaster named Frederick W. Gunn took his students hiking to a camp by the sea. It's usually considered the first organized American summer camp." Ms. Tremblay grinned. "The Gunnery camp. And you know what that means? Nobody, not once in all those years, showed up already knowing everything." Peyton felt her ambition sharpen, the real kind, not the kind you announce. She hurried down the dock toward the van, and when a girl leaned out the window and asked if she was new, Peyton said, "First year. Just like everybody was, once."

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: A short silent pause in place of 'um' or 'uh' makes a speaker sound more confident and gives listeners time to take in the point.
story:
Maelie stood at the far end of Grandma's porch, facing twelve folding chairs that held nobody but a fat orange cat. On Monday she had to give a two-minute speech in Ms. Somsak's class, with an opening hook, three points, and a closing, and every time she practiced, the same sticky little word crawled out of her mouth. "Um." She said it again now, to the cat, who blinked.

Melodie arrived on her bike with a notebook and a plan. Her own want was no secret: she wanted to be the class statistician someday, so she collected numbers about everything, and today she had chosen Maelie. "You talk," Melodie said, settling into a chair, "and I count your 'um's. Ismail said he'd text me his count from your practice yesterday." She held up her phone, where a message from Ismail read: "I counted 23 ums and also she said uh 11 times. Also tell her a wombat is a marsupial, not a rodent, because that is her second point and she keeps getting it wrong." Maelie laughed so hard she had to sit down on the porch step. "A wombat is absolutely a marsupial," she said. "I knew that. Sort of."

She tried again. Hook: imagine a wombat the size of a small dog, digging a hole big enough to swallow a picnic table. Point one, burrows. Point two, pouches, backward ones, which was genuinely strange. Point three, slow metabolism. Melodie's pencil tapped the page at every stumble, and by the closing, Maelie had watched the tally climb to nineteen. Nineteen in two minutes. She stared at the marks, which looked like a fence growing across the page, and something clicked. She had been saying "um" to fill the space while her brain caught up. What if the space just stayed space?

"Nobody counts silences," she said slowly. "You can't tally a pause." Melodie grinned and wrote a new heading at the top of a fresh page: SILENT PAUSES, SUSPICIOUSLY UNCOUNTABLE. Maelie started over. When her mind went blank before point two, she closed her mouth, let the quiet sit for a moment, and found the next word waiting behind it. The pause felt enormous from her side of it, like standing at the edge of a swimming pool, but Melodie's pencil barely moved. There were only three marks by the end, and the cat had gone to sleep, which Maelie chose to take as an insult to her wombat material and nothing more.

"Better," Melodie said, flipping back and forth between the pages. "And honestly, when you stopped, I had a second to actually picture the picnic table falling in the hole. Before, you were talking so fast I couldn't see anything." Maelie folded Ismail's note along its creases and put it in her pocket. Monday, twelve real chairs, Ms. Somsak with her stopwatch, and a hole shaped exactly like an "um" that she was no longer going to fill.

"Do the backward pouch part again," Melodie said, pencil hovering. "Slower this time. I want to draw it."

fact: In Chinese, the word for 'four' sounds very similar to the word for 'death', so some buildings in East Asia skip the fourth floor.
story:
Jackson pressed every button on Mrs. Chen's elevator panel twice, just to be sure, and the numbers still ran one, two, three, five. He was supposed to bring a birthday gift up to apartment 4B by three o'clock, and three o'clock was twenty minutes away.

"Four's bad luck," said Diego, who lived on the sixth floor and had volunteered to guide him through the building's customs. "In Chinese, the word for four sounds a lot like the word for death. So some buildings around here just skip it."

Jackson stared at the panel. He counted again, moving his finger along the row like he was reading a sentence with a word missing. Maybe, he thought, the fourth floor was still there, only wearing a disguise. He pushed five.

The doors opened on a hallway with a window overlooking the courtyard below. Jackson leaned out and looked down, counting the rows of balconies. One, two, three, and then a row that existed but had no number anywhere on it. There it was. The fourth floor was real; it had simply gone into hiding.

"Apartment 4B is probably labelled 5B," Jackson said. "Or maybe 3A plus one. It's a factor of how they count, not how they build." Diego shrugged in a way that suggested he'd known this the whole time.

They found the door marked 5B between two others and knocked. Mrs. Chen opened it, took the gift in both hands, and bowed slightly, which Jackson copied, nearly bonking his head on hers. At the table she served noodles, and Diego whispered, "Don't stick your chopsticks straight up in the bowl." Jackson laid his flat across the rim like a bridge, and Mrs. Chen smiled so wide it seemed to magnify the whole small kitchen.

"Endangered species crackers," Jackson read off the tin he'd brought. "They're shaped like pandas."

Mrs. Chen laughed. "Pandas are lucky. Come, sit, before the noodles get cold."

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
knowledge_domain: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
fact: A character's words are not always the author's view, because a novel may show a character's opinion only to argue against it.
story:
Aiden had read the same paragraph four times, and the quotation still sat there in his notebook like it belonged to someone smarter than him. "Only the strong survive," he had copied from page 112 of The Cold Valley, because it sounded important, like the kind of line a teacher would underline. He was curled in the window seat of the reading nook, the one his dad had built between two bookshelves, with a blanket over his knees and rain ticking against the glass. His assignment was to find the theme of the novel and back it up with one quotation from the text, and Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya had written "Dig deeper" on his last attempt in green pen.

Kaley arrived at four with her own copy of the book under her arm and a bag of pretzels. She squeezed into the nook beside him, bumping the lamp so it wobbled, and read his notebook upside down. "Wait. Who says that line?"

"The main bully," Aiden said. "Dorn. It's when he shoves the smaller kid off the bridge."

Kaley flipped her book open to page 112 and ran her finger down the page. "So Dorn says only the strong survive, and then what happens to Dorn?"

Aiden had to admit he hadn't thought about it that way. He accelerated through the last three chapters, skimming for the parts he'd rushed, and there it was: Dorn alone at the end, abandoned in the snow, while the smaller kid led everyone else down a safer pass. He sat back against the bookshelf. The bully's line wasn't the author talking. The whole book was arguing against it. A character's words are not always the author's view, and the novel had shown Dorn's opinion only to prove it wrong. Aiden felt the insight settle in his chest, quiet and certain, like a key turning.

He crossed out his old sentence and wrote a new one: the theme was that survival comes from cooperation, and his quotation would be the smaller kid's line from the final chapter, "We carry each other or we carry nothing." He held it up for Kaley to see.

"Now that," she said, "is not extinct," and stole a pretzel from his bag.

activity: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
knowledge_domain: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
fact: Paid ads often appear at the very top of a search results page, above the unpaid results, so the first link is not necessarily the most useful one.
story:
Ella sat at the spare desk in her mother's office, next to a dilapidated printer that jammed if anyone looked at it. She was supposed to be finding a free tool to make practice math worksheets, because her quiz on fractions was Friday and she wanted extra problems to work through. Her mother had said, "Use specific keywords, not just 'math help,'" and gone back to her meeting.

Ella typed "math help" first. She got fourteen million results, a page about tutoring services, and a video of a man shouting. She tried again with "free printable fraction worksheets grade 7." That was better. At the very top of the page sat a link in a box labeled Ad, promising free worksheets. She clicked it. The site asked for a credit card before showing anything.

Gordon, who was waiting for his own mother down the hall, leaned over the divider between the desks. "Is it broken?"

"It wants money. It said free." Ella scrolled back to the results page. Under the ad box, the rest of the links had no label at all. She clicked the second link down, a plain-looking site with no credit card anywhere. It generated twenty fraction problems and printed them, although the printer groaned like it might not contribute anything except a paper jam.

"Why was the money one first?" Gordon asked. He wanted a turn on the computer to look up a component for the remote-control car he was building, and he was bouncing one foot against the desk leg.

"Maybe it paid to be there," Ella said. She looked again at the little Ad label on the top result and then at the unlabeled ones below it. "Ads often appear at the very top, above the unpaid results. So the first link isn't necessarily the most useful one." She tried a third search, "free graph paper," and checked: an ad box on top again, plain results underneath. The pattern held.

Gordon took the keyboard. "Car motor," he typed.

"Be specific," Ella said, and pulled her worksheets off the printer.
